q: What is IOE (Initial Operating Experience), and how is it typically structured?
a: IOE is your first real line flying on the airplane, conducted with a Check Pilot. It generally consists of 3 round-trip flights, starting with a mostly demonstrated flight and ending with a Line Check.

src.quote: IOE generally consists of 3 round trip flights, starting with a mostly demonstrated flight and ending with a Line Check.
src.note: IOE is where ground school and the sim meet the real line. The Fleet Captain can extend IOE flights if additional flying would be beneficial or is needed for the candidate.

q: What is the standard leg-by-leg IOE progression a candidate should expect?
a: Leg 1 Mostly Demonstrating, Leg 2 Mostly Coaching, Leg 3 Critiquing Progress, Leg 4 Critiquing & Refining, Leg 5 Evaluating Proficiency, Leg 6 Line Check.

src.quote: Leg 1: Mostly Demonstrating; Leg 2: Mostly Coaching; Leg 3: Critiquing Progress; Leg 4: Critiquing & Refining; Leg 5: Evaluating Proficiency; Leg 6: Line Check.
src.note: The Check Pilot's role shifts from demonstrating toward evaluating as you progress. Expect to be carrying the flight, not watching it, well before the line check. Knowledge, Judgement and Airmanship are continually validated per the IOE Worksheet.

q: Along with overall competency, what two categories are you evaluated on during each leg of IOE?
a: Job Tasks and Airmanship.

src.ref: IOE Expectations — Knowledge, Judgement and Airmanship Skills
src.quote: you will be evaluated on your Job Tasks and Airmanship during each leg of IOE.
src.note: Job Tasks include overall competency with Normal Procedures, administrative paperwork, pre-flight, cockpit setup, and en route tasks. Airmanship includes overall competency with airmanship skills, takeoff & departure, and approach & landing.

q: In the OE Workbook, what does it mean when a topic is highlighted in green as a "Critical Observable Item"?
a: It is an item that must be graded with a 3 or better before proceeding to the line check.

src.quote: The topics that are highlighted in green are "Critical Observable Items." These are items that must be graded with a 3 or better, before proceeding to the line check.
src.note: Know the workbook cold before OE. The instructor expects you to hold discussions, answer questions, and validate knowledge on all material within it. The questions trace to the OE Grade Sheet and the FAA-approved FOTM.

q: What is the primary purpose of the Check Pilot who conducts your IOE and Line Check?
a: To evaluate and ensure pilot proficiency, safety, and standardization; the Check Pilot conducts aircraft line checks and Operating Experience as needed.

src.quote: The Check Pilot's primary purpose is to evaluate and ensure pilot proficiency, safety, and standardization... Conduct aircraft line checks and Operating Experience as needed.
src.note: Standardization and proficiency skills evaluated include CRM, FAR knowledge, aircraft procedures, Company policies, and local area knowledge on the route structure. The Check Pilot also seeks to mentor both Captains and First Officers.

q: As a Captain on IOE, when does your full control and authority over the aircraft and crew begin and end?
a: From the time you report for that flight until released from duty. The PIC has full control and authority in the operations of the aircraft and over the crewmembers.

src.quote: The Pilot-In-Command (PIC) has full control and authority in the operations of the aircraft and over the crewmembers and other operational staff and their duties from the time the pilot reports for that flight until released from duty.
src.note: Even with a Check Pilot aboard, you are still the PIC exercising command. Being new to the line does not suspend your command authority; the Check Pilot evaluates how you exercise it.

q: A Captain new to the line still carries a leadership/mentoring duty toward the First Officer. Where is that stated, and what is it?
a: The PIC is responsible for the day-to-day development and mentoring of the SIC, sharing knowledge and experience to prepare the SIC to assume the duties of the PIC.

src.quote: Is responsible for the day-to-day development and mentoring of the Second-In-Command (SIC); and will share knowledge and experience to prepare the SIC to assume the duties of the PIC.
src.note: Captain-on-IOE CRM point: set the tone, invite the FO in, and use the crew. Your job as leader does not pause because you are learning the line.

q: What authority does the FOM confirm the PIC may exercise unilaterally?
a: The PIC may unilaterally exercise emergency authority.

src.quote: May unilaterally exercise emergency authority.
src.note: This is the backstop of command. On IOE it is rarely used, but the candidate is expected to understand it exists and that it is the PIC's alone.

q: Who has operational control of an Alaska/Hawaiian flight, and who shares responsibility for its preflight planning and Dispatch Release?
a: The PIC and the Aircraft Dispatcher jointly share operational control; they are jointly responsible for preflight planning, delay, and the Dispatch Release.

src.quote: With the Dispatcher, is responsible for preflight planning and Dispatch Release... responsible for initiation, continuation or diversion, and termination of the flight.
src.note: "Who has operational control?" is an explicit OE Workbook question (1.1.2.4). The IOE-ready answer names the joint PIC/Dispatcher relationship, not just the Captain.

q: On IOE you will run the departure briefing. What framework does the FOM use, who initiates it, and when?
a: The Threat-Based Departure Briefing / TPC: T = Threats, P = Plan, C = Considerations. The PF initiates it prior to pushback.

src.quote: Prior to pushback, the PF initiates the departure briefing... T – Threats (PM & PF); P – Plan (PF); C – Considerations (PF).
src.note: MEMORY AID: TPC = Threats, Plan, Considerations. Keep it interactive, concise, big-picture. PM identifies threats (referencing the Crew Briefing Reference Card and any airport-specific 10-7 threats); PF briefs the plan and considerations.

q: A Check Pilot boards to conduct your evaluation. Under the FOM, can the Captain deny that access?
a: No. The Captain cannot deny a Check Pilot conducting an evaluation (nor FAA Inspectors, NTSB, Secret Service, or DOD evaluators) unless the Captain exercises emergency authority per 14 CFR 121.547(a).

src.quote: The Captain cannot deny FAA Inspectors, NTSB, Secret Service, a Check Pilot conducting an evaluation, or DOD evaluator unless the Captain exercises emergency authority per 121.547(a).
src.note: All flight deck jumpseat occupants shall observe the Sterile Flight Deck policy. Useful IOE-context fact when your Check Pilot or an FAA inspector is aboard.

q: WHERE DO I FIND IT FAST: You have an engine fire on the ground and need the immediate memory/recall action items. Which publication?
a: The QRH (Quick Reference Handbook). Memory/recall items and non-normal checklists live in the QRH; on the 787 the immediate action items are on the back of the QRC.

src.ref: 787 OE Workbook 1.3.4.1 (Non-Normal Start) / 13.1.1.1.1 (Engine Failure in Cruise)
src.quote: Is there a QRH procedure for an ENG FIRE on the ground? ... Review immediate action items (787 back of QRC) for engine failure in cruise.
src.note: Fast rule: memory items and non-normal checklists = QRH. On the 787, the recall/immediate action items are on the QRC (Quick Reference Card), backed up by the QRH. Do NOT go to the FOM for a fire drill.

q: WHERE DO I FIND IT FAST: You need to know whether you can legally dispatch with a given item inoperative, and any (O) or (M) procedures. Which publication?
a: The MEL (Minimum Equipment List), together with any associated (O) operational or (M) maintenance procedures.

src.quote: What is an "(O)" procedure listed in an MEL? ... What is the difference between a white (HAL 46-1333) vs yellow (HAL 46-1333b) MEL placard? What are the 4 different repair intervals?
src.note: Fast rule: "Can I dispatch with this inop?" = MEL. An (O) means an operational procedure the crew must accomplish; know the repair-interval categories (A/B/C/D) and the crew placarding procedure.

q: WHERE DO I FIND IT FAST: You want the airport-specific engine-failure escape procedure / departure threats for a specific runway. Which publication?
a: The Jeppesen 10-7 pages (airport-specific/airport information pages), plus the Engine Failure Procedure (EFP) source for that runway.

src.ref: 787 OE Workbook 1.3.2 (FCOM Procedures Prior to Engine Start) / 5.2.7 threat list
src.quote: Where can you find the EFP for a specific runway? Anywhere else? ... any airport-specific threats identified in the 10-7, when appropriate.
src.note: Fast rule: airport-specific escape routes, notes, and threats = Jeppesen 10-7. The FOM TPC briefing (5.2.7) explicitly points the PM at 10-7 threats. General airport charts/SIDs/STARs are also in the Jepp/FD Pro suite.

q: WHERE DO I FIND IT FAST: You need dispatch fuel requirements, alternate weather minima, or operational-control policy. Which publication?
a: The FOM (Flight Operations Manual) — dispatch/fuel/alternate/operational-control policy lives there (e.g., Ch 8 Dispatch, Ch 2 Operational Control, Ch 6 ETOPS).

src.quote: Where in the FOM is the fuel planning section? ... What are the dispatch fuel requirements for Flag operations? ... Who has operational control of a flight?
src.note: Fast rule: policy, limits, dispatch, fuel, weather minima, ETOPS, operational control = FOM. The workbook repeatedly cues "Where in the FOM..." so know the chapter map: Ch 2 operational control, Ch 5 flight ops, Ch 6 ETOPS, Ch 8 dispatch.

q: WHERE DO I FIND IT FAST: You need the normal engine-start flow / system operation versus the technique and the "why" behind a maneuver. Which two publications, respectively?
a: Normal procedures and system operation are in the FCOM; techniques, rationale, and the "why" are in the FCTM (Flight Crew Training Manual).

src.ref: General good practice (FCOM vs FCTM), consistent with OE Workbook FCOM procedure tasks (1.3.2, 1.3.4.1, 9.1.1.14)
src.quote: Perform FCOM Procedures Prior to Engine Start; Complete Normal engine Start FCOM Procedure; Perform FCOM Procedure(s) Following Landing.
src.note: Fast rule: FCOM = what/how (procedures, limitations, systems). FCTM = why/technique (maneuvers, best-practice technique such as crosswind landing guidance). The OE Workbook tasks are written as "Perform FCOM Procedure..." — that is your cue the answer is in the FCOM.

q: WHERE DO I FIND IT FAST: A JCAB ramp inspector asks whether HA is authorized to perform the NADP 1 departure procedure. Which document proves authorization?
a: The OpSpecs (Operations Specifications) — the inspector will want to see the OpSpec authorizing it.

src.quote: Is HA allowed to perform the NADP 1 Departure Procedure? (Japanese JCAB Ramp Check question; they will want to see the OpSpec).
src.note: Fast rule: "Are we authorized to...?" (specific authorizations, e.g., ITP OpSpec A354, CAT II/III, RNP-AR) = OpSpecs. Know where your OpSpecs live in the EFB so you can produce them on a ramp check.

q: How does the FOM define an ETOPS operation, and what one-engine cruise speed does the 787 use to measure it?
a: ETOPS is a flight over a route containing a point farther than 60 minutes flying time from an adequate airport at an approved one-engine-inoperative cruise speed in still air. The 787 uses .84M/290 KIAS.

src.quote: flights that operate over a route that contains a point farther than 60 minutes of flying time from an adequate airport... 787 .84M/290 KIAS.
src.note: The 60 minutes assumes one engine already inoperative. A common OE Workbook item (16.1.1.7): know the 787 single-engine speed and that the 60/120/180-minute rings are measured with it.

q: For the 787, what are the maximum diversion distances at ETOPS 120 and ETOPS 180?
a: 787 ETOPS 120 = 806 nm and ETOPS 180 = 1207 nm (60-minute ring = 410 nm), all at .84M/290 KIAS.

src.ref: FOM Table 6.2.3(1) — ETOPS Area of Operations
src.note: Directly answers the OE Workbook question "What is the maximum diversion distance, ETOPS 120? ETOPS 180?" The distances are a design/planning reference, not an operational time limit on a diversion.

q: For a decompression in the ETOPS segment, to what altitude does the FOM direct an emergency descent?
a: Perform an emergency descent to 10,000 ft or MOCA/Grid MORA, whichever is higher, then proceed direct to the nearest suitable airport.

src.quote: Perform an Emergency Descent to 10,000 ft or MOCA/Grid MORA, whichever is higher... Below FL290, or sooner if cleared by ATC, proceed directly to the nearest suitable airport.
src.note: MEMORY AID: "Ten grand or the grid, whichever is higher." Turn to offset from the route using the Special Procedures for In-Flight Contingencies first. Terrain-critical (Western U.S.) has its own depressurization strategy — OE Workbook 16.1.3.2.

q: How does a B043 Dispatch Release differ from a standard international/Flag release in the fuel summary?
a: The B043 uses 45-minute and 10% reserve fuel quantities. On the fuel summary a standard Flag shows "10% RSV" and "30@1500"; a B043 shows "45@CRZ".

src.quote: The B043 Dispatch Release is the same as the international Dispatch Release, except for the 45 minute and 10% fuel quantities listed in the fuel summary. These appear as "10% RSV" and "30@1500" (standard flag) or "45@CRZ" (B043) on the fuel summary.
src.note: The OE Workbook asks "What is the difference between a B044 vs B043 flight plan?" and "special fuel requirements for a B043." Know how to read the fuel summary line on the release.

q: On IOE the check airman asks what is in the Dispatch Release package (crews call it the "Lucky 7"). Where do you confirm the required contents, and what regulation governs the dispatch release itself?
a: Confirm the company release-package contents in the FOM Preflight Planning / International Dispatch Release section; the required regulatory contents of the dispatch release are governed by 14 CFR 121.687. If you are not certain of the exact list, say "let me confirm" and pull it up rather than reciting from memory.

src.quote: Dispatch Release package ("Lucky 7") — confirm contents in FOM Preflight Planning / International Dispatch Release; the release's required regulatory contents are per 14 CFR 121.687.
src.note: The IOE point is knowing WHERE the answer lives. Do not recite a memorized seven-item list you cannot verify on the spot.
